42322.feedback: The curves intersect at $20 and 4,000 workers. Removing the above-equilibrium floor allows wage to fall toward $20, increasing quantity demanded and reducing quantity supplied along unchanged curves.

options: The budget allows only Y = 12 at X = 15; the preferred bundle is unaffordable.
The budget allows only Y = 10 at X = 15; being preferred makes the bundle feasible.
The budget allows only Y = 10 at X = 15; the preferred bundle is unaffordable.
The budget allows only Y = 12 at X = 15; being preferred makes the bundle feasible.
42602.feedback: The budget goes through A = (15, 10). Raising Y to 15 at the same X would be preferred but would lie outside the feasible set. Preference does not remove the budget constraint.

42605.q: At the smooth interior optimum shown, the price of X falls while income and Y’s price stay fixed. What is the old price ratio Px/Py, and what adjustment is initially supported at the old bundle, assuming diminishing marginal utility and an interior new optimum?
options: One; MUx/Px rises relative to MUy/Py, favoring more spending on X subject to the new budget.
Two; MUx/Px rises relative to MUy/Py, favoring more spending on X subject to the new budget.
Two; MUx/Px falls relative to MUy/Py, favoring less spending on X subject to the new budget.
One; MUx/Px falls relative to MUy/Py, favoring less spending on X subject to the new budget.
42605.feedback: The budget intercepts are 20 for X and 40 for Y, so Px/Py = 40/20 = 2. At the old tangency MUx/Px = MUy/Py. Lower Px raises MUx/Px at the unchanged bundle. Reallocation toward X helps restore equality, while the final bundle must satisfy the new budget.

Only if marginal utilities are known

No; every affordable bundle must exhaust income

42641.q: A consumer prefers A to B and B to C. What does transitivity require?
options: C must be preferred to A
A must be preferred to C
A and C must be tied
The ranking may cycle without inconsistency
42641.feedback: Transitivity makes preference rankings internally consistent: A ≻ B and B ≻ C imply A ≻ C.

42642.q: A consumer can compare every pair of feasible bundles. Which preference property is illustrated?
options: Transitivity
Convexity
Completeness
Cardinal utility
42642.feedback: Completeness means the consumer can rank any two bundles or regard them as equally preferred.

42643.q: Bundle D contains at least as much of both desirable goods as bundle E and more of one. Under more-is-better, how are they ranked?

D is strictly preferred to E

42656.q: Two distinct standard indifference curves cross. What is the strongest diagnosis?
options: The diagram violates consistent, monotonic preferences
The consumer has a larger budget
The goods must be perfect complements
The crossing measures cardinal utility
42656.feedback: A shared bundle would have to be indifferent to bundles on both curves, contradicting the ordering implied by more-is-better.

Both goods have negative prices
Income falls as consumption rises

42669.q: Utility numbers 10, 30, and 90 rank three bundles. Which inference is valid?
options: It provides exactly three times the satisfaction of 30
The bundle assigned 90 is preferred to those assigned 30 and 10
The utility gaps have dollar meaning
Utility 10 is objectively low for every person
42669.feedback: Ordinal utility preserves preference order; its magnitudes and gaps do not measure comparable amounts of satisfaction.

42670.q: Every utility number is replaced by twice that number plus five. What happens to the represented preferences?
options: Every preference reverses
Utility becomes comparable across people
The ranking is unchanged
The budget line rotates
42670.feedback: A strictly increasing transformation preserves the order of all bundle comparisons.

42671.q: Bundle A has utility 40 and bundle B has utility 20. Which conclusion is not justified by ordinal utility?
options: A is preferred to B
B has the lower assigned number
The numbers preserve a ranking
A provides exactly twice as much satisfaction as B
42671.feedback: Ordinal utility conveys order, not ratios or measurable amounts of satisfaction.

Utility is measured in dollars
Everyone must use the same numerical scale
The bundle must be unaffordable

P62B-ELAS-B2-019.q: Refer to the graph. As price falls from C through B to A, which total-revenue sequence and economic explanation are correct?

P62B-ELAS-B2-020.q: Use the graph. Refer to the common starting point and the higher marked price on the two supply curves. Which short-run and long-run quantity increases, and elasticity interpretation, are supported?

P62B-ELAS-B3-008.q: A 10 percent price increase lowers quantity 20 percent. Cost per unit is unchanged. Which revenue-profit statement is best supported?

P62B-ELAS-B3-020.q: Using the midpoint formula and the displayed short-run and long-run endpoints, which approximate pair correctly compares supply elasticity?

P62B-ELAS-E-028.q: For the marked price decrease on D1 and D2, which midpoint elasticities in absolute value and interpretation are correct?

About 1.20 for D1 and 0.75 for D2; a curve’s slope in axis units is its elasticity at every point.

P62B-ELAS-EL-033.q: Refer to the graph. Which total revenue at B and interpretation of a small movement in either direction along demand are correct?

P62B-ELAS-EL-038.q: Use the graph. Refer to the common starting point and the higher marked price on the two supply curves. Which short-run and long-run quantity increases, and elasticity interpretation, are supported?

P62B-ELAS-H-016.q: The upper and lower portions of the plotted demand curve have the same slope. Which point elasticities at C and A, and explanation, reconcile that slope with different percentage responses?

P62B-ELAS-L-091.q: Compare the C→B and B→A intervals on the graph. Why can their elasticity classifications differ?

P62C-CPS-B2-008.q: Refer to the graph. A lump-sum rule transfers $20 from buyers to sellers without changing quantity, allocation or resource costs. What is producer surplus after the transfer, and what happens to total surplus?

P62E-COP-M-024.q: Refer to the graph. What is the vertical difference between total cost and total variable cost, and why does it remain at that amount as output changes?

P62E-COP-M-026.q: Refer to the graph. Where does MC cross AVC, and what do the marginal-average relationships imply at the crossing?
options: At roughly Q = 25; the next units switch from lowering to raising the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
At roughly Q = 32; the next units switch from raising to lowering the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
At roughly Q = 25; the next units switch from raising to lowering the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
At roughly Q = 32; the next units switch from lowering to raising the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
P62E-COP-M-026.feedback: MC crosses AVC at roughly Q = 32. Before each crossing MC is below that average and pulls it down; after the crossing MC is above it and pulls it up. Thus the crossing identifies a minimum, not a maximum.

P62E-COP-M-040.q: At the labor input where total product reaches its maximum, what is marginal product?

At its maximum positive value
Equal to total product

P62F-PC-B1-005.q: Use the graph. Which approximate quantity at Q1 and marginal condition identify the firm’s profit-maximizing output?

About 60 units; MC rises through price, so extra units beyond it cost more than they add to revenue.

P62F-PC-B1-005.feedback: Q1 is near 60 on rising MC. Just below it MR = P exceeds MC; just above it MC exceeds MR. This change in marginal profit identifies a maximum, unlike a falling-MC crossing.

P62F-PC-B1-019.q: At the profit-maximizing output in the graph, what is profit per unit, and which comparison measures it?
options: $15, from price minus ATC.
$10, from price minus AVC.
$15, from price minus AVC.
$10, from price minus ATC.
P62F-PC-B1-019.feedback: Rising MC meets price at Q = 50. Price is $30, ATC $20 and AVC $10. Profit per unit is P−ATC = $10; P−AVC instead measures contribution toward fixed cost.

P62F-PC-B1-020.q: Refer to the graph. Which price and price–cost comparison establish that the firm breaks even at its profit-maximizing output?

$25; P = ATC gives zero economic profit while covering the normal return included in economic cost.
$25; P = ATC means the owner’s opportunity cost and normal return are not covered.
$20; P = ATC means the owner’s opportunity cost and normal return are not covered.
P62F-PC-B1-020.feedback: The firm chooses Q = 50 at P = MC = 25, and ATC is also 25. Revenue covers all economic costs, including implicit opportunity costs; zero economic profit is break-even, not no return.

P62F-PC-B2-024.q: At Q1 in the graph, what is the approximate height of the profit rectangle, and what does that height measure?

between $10 and $15 per unit; price minus ATC measures economic profit per unit.
between $10 and $15 per unit; the vertical gap alone is total economic profit.
between $6 and $10 per unit; the vertical gap alone is total economic profit.

P62F-PC-B2-037.q: Which operating loss and shutdown loss are implied by the graph, and what should the firm do if fixed cost is unavoidable?

$1,500; entry reduces market supply and raises each survivor’s price and output until profit is zero.

P62F-PC-B3-058.q: Starting with market price in the paired market and firm diagram, which firm output and cost relationships summarize the long-run competitive equilibrium?

P62F-PC-EL-033.q: At the chosen output, what is the price–AVC margin, and why does the graph show break-even rather than the shutdown threshold?

P62F-PC-EL-034.q: Which operating loss and shutdown loss are implied by the graph, and what should the firm do if fixed cost is unavoidable?
options: Operate: lose $200; shut down: lose $500. Producing covers variable cost and part of fixed cost.
Operate: lose $300; shut down: lose $600. A loss alone requires shutdown regardless of the avoidable-cost comparison.
Operate: lose $300; shut down: lose $600. Producing covers variable cost and part of fixed cost.
Operate: lose $200; shut down: lose $500. A loss alone requires shutdown regardless of the avoidable-cost comparison.

P62F-PC-EL-036.q: At what price does the positive-output portion of short-run supply begin in the graph, and why is lower MC excluded?

$20 at A; lower prices do not cover minimum AVC.

$30 at B; any positive MC guarantees that producing covers total cost.

P62F-PC-EL-037.q: Use the graph. Fixed cost falls while MC and AVC remain as drawn. What happens to the shutdown price, and why?

It remains $20; fixed cost is the avoidable cost that determines shutdown.
It remains $20; minimum AVC, not fixed cost, sets the operating threshold.

P62F-PC-EL-039.q: Use the graph. Which plotted market and firm quantities and interpretation respect the difference between the panels?

P62F-PC-EL-040.q: As exit raises market price with the surviving firm’s costs fixed, which initial quantity and output response are supported by the graph?

40 units; the price increase shifts MC rather than changing the chosen point on it.

P62F-PC-EL-042.q: Use the graph. Which market and firm quantities are plotted, and why is dividing them insufficient to establish an exact firm count?

75 thousand and 50; a representative-firm drawing by itself proves every firm has that identical output.

P62F-PC-EL-043.q: Use the graph. How do the two panels determine the representative firm’s price and output?

The market sets price at about $25; the firm takes it as horizontal MR and selects output on rising MC.
The market sets price at about $25; the firm uses the whole market quantity as its own output regardless of MC.
The market sets price at about $20; the firm uses the whole market quantity as its own output regardless of MC.

P62F-PC-EL-044.q: Which price and firm output in the paired market and firm diagram, together with the economic conditions, establish a long-run competitive benchmark rather than only current break-even?
options: P = $20, Q = 40; P = MC = minimum ATC gives zero economic profit and no net entry or exit pressure.
P = $25, Q = 50; P = AVC alone establishes long-run break-even and removes all entry or exit pressure.
P = $25, Q = 50; P = MC = minimum ATC gives zero economic profit and no net entry or exit pressure.
P = $20, Q = 40; P = AVC alone establishes long-run break-even and removes all entry or exit pressure.
P62F-PC-EL-044.feedback: The market supplies price 25 to the firm. Its rising MC crosses at Q = 50, also the ATC minimum. P = MC gives marginal efficiency; P = min ATC gives productive efficiency and zero economic profit. Covering AVC alone is only a short-run operating criterion.

P62F-PC-H-011.q: Use the graph. Which price reading and order of analysis correctly determine the firm’s output and profit?
options: Price is between $35 and $40; use rising MC = P to choose output, then compare P with ATC there.
Price is between $40 and $45; use rising MC = P to choose output, then compare P with ATC there.

P62F-PC-H-012.q: Which market price and short-run decision are supported by the graph?

$20; produce at the rising-MC intersection despite an economic loss because price covers AVC.

$22; shut down because price below ATC is sufficient for shutdown.

P62F-PC-H-013.q: Which price reading and operating decision are supported by the graph?

P62F-PC-H-014.q: At the price shown, which profit and productive-efficiency conclusions follow from the firm’s cost curves?

options: Between $20 and $25; operate now because price covers AVC, then exit raises survivors’ MR and output until losses disappear.
Between $25 and $30; operate now because price covers AVC, then exit raises survivors’ MR and output until losses disappear.
Between $20 and $25; covering AVC now eliminates any long-run incentive to exit despite persistent losses.
Between $25 and $30; covering AVC now eliminates any long-run incentive to exit despite persistent losses.
P62F-PC-L-065.feedback: Price is near 21 at Q1, above AVC but below ATC. Current operation covers some fixed cost. Later exit reduces market supply, raising price and each survivor’s horizontal MR; with unchanged cost curves, output rises along MC until total costs are covered.

P62F-PC-L-066.q: Which price reading and operating decision are supported by the graph?
options: $10; shut down because price is below minimum AVC, bearing unavoidable fixed cost.
$14; shut down because price is below minimum AVC, bearing unavoidable fixed cost.
$14; produce at a price–MC crossing even though no positive output covers variable cost.
$10; produce at a price–MC crossing even though no positive output covers variable cost.
P62F-PC-L-066.feedback: The price line is 14, below minimum AVC near 19. At any positive output revenue fails to cover variable cost. Shutdown avoids that extra loss, but fixed cost remains.

P62F-PC-L-067.q: What is the approximate shutdown-price threshold in the graph, and which part of MC supplies the firm’s positive short-run output?
options: $20; rising MC at and above minimum AVC.
$16; the entire MC curve, including prices below minimum AVC.
$16; rising MC at and above minimum AVC.
$20; the entire MC curve, including prices below minimum AVC.

P62F-PC-L-068.q: Use the graph. How do the two panels determine the representative firm’s price and output?
options: The market sets price at about $35; the firm takes it as horizontal MR and selects output on rising MC.
The market sets price at about $45; the firm uses the whole market quantity as its own output regardless of MC.
The market sets price at about $35; the firm uses the whole market quantity as its own output regardless of MC.

P62F-PC-L-069.q: Use the graph. Which approximate final price P2 and explanation of the long-run adjustment are correct?

P62F-PC-L-070.q: Use the graph. Which approximate final price P2 and explanation of the long-run adjustment are correct?

P62F-PC-L-072.q: At industry quantity 80, which approximate long-run price and cost interpretation are supported by the graph?

$48; rising long-run price must reflect lower minimum firm costs.

$30; P = MC establishes productive efficiency and P = minimum ATC is the definition of allocative efficiency.
P62F-PC-L-074.feedback: At Q1 the horizontal price near 24 meets MC and the ATC minimum. The first equality matches marginal value and cost; the second achieves the lowest average cost. These are distinct efficiency concepts.

P62F-PC-L-075.q: Demand rises from D1 to D2 in the increasing-cost industry shown. Which approximate new long-run price and explanation of its relation to the original price are correct?

$50; expansion raises firms’ costs, so entry does not restore the original lower break-even price.

In an increasing-cost industry, entry lowers price from its initial short-run peak but higher input costs leave the new long-run price above the original. The figure shows long-run intersections, not the size of the short-run peak.

P62F-PC-L-091.q: Which calculation and sequence correctly determine economic profit from the graph?

$500; choose Q = 50 from rising MC = P, then multiply the price–ATC gap by output.

P62F-PC-L-092.q: At the price shown in the graph, how should the firm interpret its economic profit and the return included in total economic cost?

$30; the firm necessarily earns zero economic profit and avoids all fixed cost.

A/X alone is an equilibrium; its joint profit 23 versus 21 at B/Y makes B/Y fail the Nash condition even without a profitable unilateral deviation.
A/Y alone is an equilibrium; its joint profit 23 versus 21 at B/X makes B/X fail the Nash condition even without a profitable unilateral deviation.
A/X and B/Y are equilibria; A/X has joint profit 23 versus 21 at B/Y, but the larger total does not eliminate B/Y as an equilibrium.
P62I-OLI-L-004.feedback: At A/X, neither Row (14 versus 1) nor Column (9 versus 2) wants to deviate. At B/Y, neither Row (8 versus 2) nor Column (13 versus 1) wants to deviate. The totals are 23 and 21. Nash equilibrium concerns unilateral incentives, not whether another cell has a larger sum.

P62I-OLI-L-010.q: In the delivery-slot matrix, payoffs are ordered (Row, Column). Which joint-payoff reading and pure-equilibrium assessment are correct?
options: Every cell totals 10; none is a pure equilibrium because every cell permits a profitable unilateral deviation.
Every cell totals 8; none is a pure equilibrium because every cell permits a profitable unilateral deviation.
Every cell totals 8; all are pure equilibria because equal joint totals eliminate unilateral incentives.
Every cell totals 10; all are pure equilibria because equal joint totals eliminate unilateral incentives.
P62I-OLI-L-010.feedback: The cells are (6, 2), (2, 6), (2, 6), (6, 2), all totaling 8. Row prefers A against X and B against Y; Column prefers Y against A and X against B. Each pure cell has a profitable deviation. Equal sums do not imply mutual best responses.

P62I-OLI-L-072.q: Rivals match fare cuts but not fare increases in the kinked-demand market shown. Constant MC rises from $48 to $54, with demand and fixed cost unchanged. Which fare, quantity and profit assessment follow?
options: Fare $72 and quantity 20 remain unchanged; profit falls $120 because MC stays within the MR gap.
Fare $72 and quantity 30 remain unchanged; profit is unchanged because price rigidity prevents costs from affecting profit.
Fare $72 and quantity 20 remain unchanged; profit is unchanged because price rigidity prevents costs from affecting profit.
Fare $72 and quantity 30 remain unchanged; profit falls $180 because MC stays within the MR gap.
P62I-OLI-L-072.feedback: The kink is at Q 30, P 72 and the MR gap 36–60. Both cost levels lie inside it, so output and price stay fixed. Costs rise 6 × 30 = $180, reducing economic profit by that amount.
P62I-OLI-L-072.imageAlt: Kinked demand at quantity 30, price 72, with two MR branches and MC at 48.
P62I-OLI-L-072.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. Demand follows P=84−0.4Q for Q up to 30, then P=108−1.2Q for larger Q. At Q=30, the upper MR branch ends at 60 and the lower branch begins at 36. MC is horizontal at 48.

P62I-OLI-L-073.q: Using the kinked demand and MR shown, compare raising constant MC to $45 with raising it to $55. Hold demand fixed. Which results and explanation are correct?
options: At $45: Q = 20, P = $60; at $55: Q = 15, P = $62.50. The first cost lies within the MR gap, while the second lies above it.
At $45: Q = 30, P = $60; at $55: Q = 25, P = $62.50. The first cost lies within the MR gap, while the second lies above it.
At $45: Q = 20, P = $60; at $55: Q = 15, P = $62.50. Any cost change inside the MR gap must change the profit-maximizing quantity.
At $45: Q = 30, P = $60; at $55: Q = 25, P = $62.50. Any cost change inside the MR gap must change the profit-maximizing quantity.
P62I-OLI-L-073.feedback: The kink is (20, 60) with MR dropping 50→30. MC 45 lies in the gap and keeps the kink optimal. The upper MR branch is 70−Q; MC 55 gives Q = 15 and P = 70−0.5 × 15 = 62.50. Rigidity applies within the gap, not to every cost change.
P62I-OLI-L-073.imageAlt: Kinked demand at quantity 20, price 60, with two MR branches and MC at 40.
P62I-OLI-L-073.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. Demand follows P=70−0.5Q for Q up to 20, then P=90−1.5Q for larger Q. At Q=20, the upper MR branch ends at 50 and the lower branch begins at 30. MC is horizontal at 40.

P62I-OLI-L-074.q: The firm starts at the kink shown. An input improvement lowers constant MC from $48 to $42, while a recurring license fee adds $300 to fixed cost. Demand is unchanged and the firm stays active. Which evaluation is correct?
options: Price and quantity stay at $72 and 20; the $120 variable-cost saving is smaller than the fee, reducing profit $180.
Price and quantity stay at $72 and 30; the $180 variable-cost saving is smaller than the fee, reducing profit $120.
Price and quantity stay at $72 and 30; the $300 fixed fee must enter MC and outweigh the $180 saving in the output rule.
Price and quantity stay at $72 and 20; the $300 fixed fee must enter MC and outweigh the $120 saving in the output rule.
P62I-OLI-L-074.feedback: The kink is Q 30, P 72 with MR gap 36–60. MC 42 remains in the gap. Variable-cost savings are (48−42) × 30 = $180, less than the 300 fee, so profit falls 120. The fixed fee affects profit, not the marginal output decision.
P62I-OLI-L-074.imageAlt: Kinked demand at quantity 30, price 72, with two MR branches and MC at 48.
P62I-OLI-L-074.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. Demand follows P=84−0.4Q for Q up to 30, then P=108−1.2Q for larger Q. At Q=30, the upper MR branch ends at 60 and the lower branch begins at 36. MC is horizontal at 48.

P62I-OLI-LB-007.q: Starting from the displayed matrix, a program adds 6 to each firm’s payoff only at A/X. All other payoffs stay fixed. Which pure equilibria and joint-payoff conclusion follow?
options: A/X and B/Y are both equilibria; A/X has the highest joint payoff, 32.
A/X and B/Y are both equilibria; A/X has the highest joint payoff, 36.
Only A/X is an equilibrium; its highest joint payoff of 32 automatically eliminates the unchanged B/Y equilibrium.
Only A/X is an equilibrium; its highest joint payoff of 36 automatically eliminates the unchanged B/Y equilibrium.
P62I-OLI-LB-007.feedback: A/X becomes (16, 16); each prefers 16 there to the 14 from deviating. B/Y remains (7, 7), where deviating gives either player 5. Both are mutual best responses. A/X totals 32, the highest total, but that does not erase B/Y’s unilateral stability.

P62I-OLI-LB-021.q: Use the graph’s plotted demand and constant MC. Two identical cartel members split the joint-profit-maximizing output equally. One secretly adds one unit while the other holds its quota. Which profit comparison and incentive assessment are correct?
options: The deviator gains $14 while joint profit falls $2; the deviation is privately attractive despite harming the cartel.
The deviator gains $18 while joint profit falls $2; lower joint profit by itself removes the unilateral incentive.
The deviator gains $18 while joint profit falls $2; the deviation is privately attractive despite harming the cartel.
The deviator gains $14 while joint profit falls $2; lower joint profit by itself removes the unilateral incentive.
P62I-OLI-LB-021.feedback: Demand is P = 100−2 Q and MC = $20. MR = MC gives Q = 20, P = 60 and each member profit (60−20) × 10 = $400. Deviation gives Q = 21, P = 58 and deviator profit (58−20) × 11 = $418. Joint profit falls from $800 to $798. Individual incentives differ from the joint objective.

P62I-OLI-LB-024.q: Use the graph. The cartel faces the plotted demand and constant MC. Demand price falls $2.50 for each extra unit of total output. Two members split cartel output equally; one adds two units while the other holds its quota. Which incentive and deterrence threshold follow?
options: The deviator gains $35 and joint profit falls $10; an expected present-value punishment greater than $35 deters it.
The deviator gains $45 and joint profit falls $10; an expected present-value punishment greater than $45 deters it.
The deviator gains $45 and joint profit falls $10; a punishment just above the $10 joint loss is sufficient.
The deviator gains $35 and joint profit falls $10; a punishment just above the $10 joint loss is sufficient.
P62I-OLI-LB-024.feedback: The intercept is 140 and MC 30, so joint MR = 140−5 Q gives Q = 22, P 85. Each earns (85−30) × 11 = 605. Deviation gives total Q = 24, P 80 and deviator output 13, profit 650, a gain 45. Joint profit falls 1210→1200. Deterrence compares the deviator’s own gain with its expected discounted penalty.

P62I-OLI-LB-027.q: Use the demand and MC in the cartel graph. Compare a $200 lump-sum license charge with a $10 tax per unit. The cartel remains active and reoptimizes jointly. Which net profits and output effects are correct?
options: License: $600; unit tax: $612.50. Only the unit tax changes MR = MC and the chosen output.
License: $500; unit tax: $512.50. Only the unit tax changes MR = MC and the chosen output.
License: $600; unit tax: $612.50. The license changes marginal cost, while the unit tax leaves it unchanged.
License: $500; unit tax: $512.50. The license changes marginal cost, while the unit tax leaves it unchanged.
P62I-OLI-LB-027.feedback: The figure gives P = 100−2 Q and MC = 20. Original Q = 20, P = 60, profit 800. A fixed $200 charge leaves Q unchanged and profit 600. The unit tax raises effective MC to 30: Q = 17.5, P = 65, profit = (65−30) × 17.5 = 612.50. A fixed charge reduces profit without entering MC.

PG1-SUP-L-001.q: Use the graph. A producer claims that the move from A to B proves that supply increased. Which quantity change and diagnosis are correct?
options: An increase of 100 thousand units; this is a change in quantity supplied along the existing curve.
An increase of 125 thousand units; any rise in quantity is an increase in the whole supply schedule.
An increase of 100 thousand units; any rise in quantity is an increase in the whole supply schedule.
An increase of 125 thousand units; this is a change in quantity supplied along the existing curve.
PG1-SUP-L-001.feedback: A is at 100 thousand units and B at 225 thousand, an increase of 125 thousand. Both lie on the same supply curve. The higher own price changes quantity supplied; an increase in supply would shift the entire schedule.

PMC-COP-R-010.q: A learner says, “If the owner did not write a check, the resource has no cost.” Which statement corrects this claim?
options: Only variable resources have economic costs
Every implicit cost must appear on an invoice
Opportunity cost matters only for consumers
Owner-supplied resources can have implicit opportunity costs even without a cash payment
PMC-COP-R-010.feedback: Economic cost includes the value of the next-best use of owner-supplied resources.

PMC-COP-R-025.q: A learner calls zero economic profit a “loss.” Which statement corrects this claim?
options: Zero economic profit means all explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit, are covered
Zero economic profit means revenue is zero
Zero economic profit means explicit costs exceed revenue
Zero economic profit excludes owner compensation
PMC-COP-R-025.feedback: Normal profit is included in economic cost, so zero economic profit can be a sustainable outcome.

PMC-COP-R-068.q: A learner says AFC eventually rises because “all U-shaped costs rise.” Which statement corrects this claim?
options: AFC rises whenever MC rises
AFC keeps falling as fixed cost is spread over more output
AFC is U-shaped like AVC
AFC equals MC at its minimum
PMC-COP-R-068.feedback: AFC is not U-shaped in the standard model; it declines as quantity increases.

PMC-COP-R-117.q: A learner says, “Fixed cost and sunk cost mean the same thing.” Which statement corrects this claim?
options: A fixed cost can be avoidable in a future decision; a sunk cost is unrecoverable
Every sunk cost varies with output
Every fixed cost has already been paid forever
Sunk costs are always implicit
PMC-COP-R-117.feedback: Fixed describes how cost behaves with current output; sunk describes whether it can be recovered.

PMS-ELAS-R-029.q: A learner says labor demand elasticity is unrelated to substitution possibilities. Which statement corrects this mistake?
options: More available substitutes for a type of labor generally make labor demand more elastic
Substitutes make labor demand perfectly inelastic
Factor demand elasticity depends only on worker preferences
Substitution changes labor supply but never labor demand
PMS-ELAS-R-029.feedback: Employers can respond more strongly to wage changes when alternative inputs are available.
